title: Dynamic Programming: Longest Increasing Subsequence
oneLiner: For every index, the best increasing run ENDING there only depends on the best runs ending at every SMALLER, earlier value -- the same overlapping-subproblem shape as Climbing Stairs, one dimension wider.
keyTakeaway: dp[i] = the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS at index i (not just "up to i") -- computed as 1 + the best dp[j] among every earlier j where nums[j] < nums[i], or just 1 if no such j exists. The answer to the whole problem is the MAXIMUM value anywhere in the finished dp array, not dp[n-1] -- the longest increasing run doesn't have to end at the last element.
explanation:
A subsequence keeps elements in their original order but doesn't require them to be adjacent -- [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7] has the increasing subsequence [2, 5, 7] (skipping 10, 9, and 3) even though those three values aren't next to each other. "Longest Increasing Subsequence" asks for the length of the longest such run.

The DP insight: define dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS exactly at index i (using nums[i] as its last element, not just anywhere up to i). To compute dp[i], look at every earlier index j: if nums[j] < nums[i], then nums[i] could extend whatever increasing run ends at j, giving a candidate length of dp[j] + 1. dp[i] is the best (maximum) of all those candidates, or just 1 on its own if nothing earlier is smaller (every single element is trivially an increasing subsequence of length 1).

This is the same "break a problem into smaller already-solved subproblems" shape as Climbing Stairs, just checking ALL earlier indices instead of only the two right before it -- which is what makes this O(n^2) instead of O(n). One easy mistake: the final answer isn't dp[n-1] (the last cell) -- it's the MAXIMUM value anywhere in the dp array, since the longest run doesn't have to end at the array's last element at all.

Watch dp fill left to right below -- each cell shows which earlier, smaller value it extended (or that it started fresh at length 1), and the tracker shows the best length found so far across the whole array.

visualizationSteps.message: dp[0] (value 10): no earlier smaller value to extend, so dp[0] = 1.
dp[1] (value 9): no earlier smaller value to extend, so dp[1] = 1.
dp[2] (value 2): no earlier smaller value to extend, so dp[2] = 1.
dp[3] (value 5): best extension is index 2 (value 2 < 5), so dp[3] = dp[2] + 1 = 2.
dp[4] (value 3): best extension is index 2 (value 2 < 3), so dp[4] = dp[2] + 1 = 2.
dp[5] (value 7): best extension is index 3 (value 5 < 7), so dp[5] = dp[3] + 1 = 3.
Done -- longest increasing subsequence length is max(dp) = 3.

recognitionSignals: The problem asks for the longest/shortest run, subsequence, or subset that must stay in ORDER but doesn't require adjacency -- "subsequence" (not "subarray" or "substring") is the signal word.

A greedy "just track the running best" approach doesn't work because an early bad choice can block a better later run -- you need to know the best answer ending at EVERY index, not just the overall best so far.
gotchas: The answer is max(dp), not dp[n-1] -- the longest increasing run can end anywhere in the array, not necessarily at the last element.
dp[i] means "ends AT i," not "best subsequence somewhere in the first i elements" -- mixing those two definitions up breaks the recurrence.
confusableWith: 0/1 Knapsack (patterns track) is also "build a dp array from smaller solved subproblems," but Knapsack's state is a fixed capacity dimension, not "which earlier index did I extend."

complexity.note: For each of n positions, scan every earlier position (n²/2 pairs); the dp array is n cells. (A cleverer binary-search approach reaches O(n log n).)
